claim: Drosophila has three larval stages in development, L1-L3.
source: There are three larval stages in the development of Drosophila, L1–L3 (Szabad et al., 1979; Dambly-Chaudière and Ghysen, 1986; Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Each segment of the abdominal epidermis has a belt of thorny denticles ventrally.
source: Ventrally, each segment of the abdominal epidermis has a belt of thorny denticles (Lohs-Schardin et al., 1979; Dougan and DiNardo, 1992; Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997; Payre et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: Each denticle belt is built by seven lines of cells.
source: Each belt is built by seven lines of cells (Figure 1) that together produce seven imperfectly defined rows of denticles (Price et al., 2006; Walters et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is stated in text with reference to Figure 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Denticle rows 0 and 1 are made by cells of the posterior compartment (P).
source: denticle rows 0 and 1 are made by cells of the posterior compartment (P) (Dougan and DiNardo, 1992)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Denticle rows 2-7 are made by cells of the anterior compartment (A).
source: rows 2–7 by the anterior compartment (A).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text following the discussion of compartment organization.

claim: Denticles in rows 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 point backwards.
source: The denticles in rows 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 point backwards while those in rows 0, 1 and 4 point forwards (Lohs-Schardin et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Denticles in rows 0, 1 and 4 point forwards.
source: The denticles in rows 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 point backwards while those in rows 0, 1 and 4 point forwards (Lohs-Schardin et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Cells that make denticle rows 2 and 5 in the embryo are tendon cells that link epidermal cells to muscles.
source: The cells that make denticle rows 2 and 5 in the embryo have also an additional function: they are the tendon cells that link epidermal cells to muscles (Figure 1C–E; Hatini and DiNardo, 2001; Volohonsky et al., 2007; reviewed in Volk (1999)).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1 and supported by multiple citations.

claim: During each moult cycle, the larval epidermis secretes a new cuticle under the old one.
source: During each moult cycle, the larval epidermis secretes a new cuticle under the old one and when this process is completed, the old cuticle is sloughed off.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a description of the moulting process.

claim: Over the two larval moult cycles the epidermal cells do not change in number.
source: Over the two larval moult cycles the epidermal cells do not change in number, but they undergo endoreplication of their DNA and grow considerably (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: Epidermal cells undergo endoreplication of their DNA and grow considerably over the two larval moult cycles.
source: Over the two larval moult cycles the epidermal cells do not change in number, but they undergo endoreplication of their DNA and grow considerably (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: During embryogenesis, actin-based pre-denticles are formed temporarily at the apico-posterior limits of the cells and all point backwards.
source: During embryogenesis, the actin-based pre-denticles, the precursors of the cuticular denticles, are formed temporarily at the apico-posterior limits of the cells and all point backwards (Figure 1A; Dickinson and Thatcher, 1997).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1A and supported by a citation.

claim: By the L1 stage the completed denticles of rows 1 and 4 point forwards.
source: However, by the L1 stage the completed denticles of rows 1 and 4 now point forwards (Figure 1E; Lohs-Schardin et al., 1979)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1E and supported by a citation.

claim: Rows 1 and 4 have broader cells and start to behave differently from the other rows shortly before stage 16, at the beginning of cuticle formation.
source: However, our observations suggest that rows 1 and 4 have broader cells and start to behave differently from the other rows shortly before stage 16, at the beginning of cuticle formation (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' observations and supported by reference to Figure 2A.

claim: In both pre-L2 and pre-L3 stages the pre-denticles of rows 1 and 4 point forwards.
source: The pre-denticles do not all point backwards: in both pre-L2 and pre-L3 stages the pre-denticles of rows 1 and 4 point forwards (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Row 0 denticles are present in only the L2 and L3 stages.
source: Row 0 denticles, which are present in only the L2 and L3 stages, also come from pre-denticles that point anteriorly.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Row 0 denticles come from pre-denticles that point anteriorly.
source: Row 0 denticles, which are present in only the L2 and L3 stages, also come from pre-denticles that point anteriorly.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: All the larval pre-denticles are an accurate harbinger of the orientation of the denticles that they will make.
source: Therefore, unlike the embryonic pre-denticles, all the larval pre-denticles are an accurate harbinger of the orientation of the denticles that they will make.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: The larva grows substantially and moults twice with only subtle changes to the pattern.
source: The larva grows substantially and moults twice with only subtle changes to the pattern (Dambly-Chaudière and Ghysen, 1986; Hartenstein and Campos-Ortega, 1986).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: Larval epidermal cells become polytene as they do in Calliphora.
source: It has been assumed that the cells become polytene as they do in Calliphora (Pearson, 1974), and that they neither divide nor die.
evidence: The claim is stated as an assumption in the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Larval epidermal cells neither divide nor die.
source: It has been assumed that the cells become polytene as they do in Calliphora (Pearson, 1974), and that they neither divide nor die.
evidence: The claim is stated as an assumption in the literature.

claim: It was expected that the arrangement of the cells as well as their identities are conserved throughout the three larval stages.
source: These assumptions led to the reasonable expectations that the arrangement of the cells as well as their identities are conserved throughout the three larval stages (Szabad et al., 1979; Dambly-Chaudière and Ghysen, 1986; Hartenstein and Campos-Ortega, 1986; Bate and Martínez Arias, 1993; Campos-Ortega and Hartenstein, 1997).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an expectation based on prior assumptions, supported by citations.

claim: Both the arrangement of cells and their identities are not conserved throughout the three larval stages.
source: However, as we now demonstrate, both these expectations are mistaken.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a finding that contradicts prior expectations.

claim: In the embryo, the lines of epidermal cells that will produce the denticles of L1 are more tightly compacted than those cells that do not produce denticles.
source: In the embryo, the lines of epidermal cells that will produce the denticles of L1 are more tightly compacted than those cells that do not produce denticles (Price et al., 2006; Walters et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: In the embryo, tendon cells make the pre-denticles of rows 2 and 5.
source: and include tendon cells that themselves make the pre-denticles of rows 2 and 5 (Figures 1C and 2; Hatini and DiNardo, 2001).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to figures and supported by a citation.

claim: The tendon cells are separated by the two lines of cells that will make denticle rows 3 and 4 in the embryo.
source: The tendon cells are separated by the two lines of cells that will make denticle rows 3 and 4 (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: The embryonic P compartment is two-cells wide in the anteroposterior axis.
source: The embryonic P compartment is two-cells wide in the anteroposterior axis, the posterior of these two lines of cells making row 1 denticles (Figure 1A,G; Dougan and DiNardo, 1992).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: The posterior line of cells in the embryonic P compartment makes row 1 denticles.
source: The embryonic P compartment is two-cells wide in the anteroposterior axis, the posterior of these two lines of cells making row 1 denticles (Figure 1A,G; Dougan and DiNardo, 1992).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated with reference to Figure 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: Unlike the tendon cells of the embryo, the tendon cells of the larva do not themselves make denticles.
source: first, unlike the tendon cells of the embryo, the tendon cells of the larva do not themselves make denticles.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a difference between embryo and larva.

claim: One row of tendon cells is located between denticle rows 1 and 2 in the larva.
source: One row of tendon cells is located between denticle rows 1 and 2 and the other between denticle rows 4 and 5 (Figure 1B,D,F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: One row of tendon cells is located between denticle rows 4 and 5 in the larva.
source: One row of tendon cells is located between denticle rows 1 and 2 and the other between denticle rows 4 and 5 (Figure 1B,D,F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: In the embryo there are two lines of cells between the tendon cells.
source: Second, in the embryo there are two lines of cells between the tendon cells, while in the larva the tendon cells are separated by three lines of cells.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a comparison between embryo and larva.

claim: In the larva the tendon cells are separated by three lines of cells.
source: Second, in the embryo there are two lines of cells between the tendon cells, while in the larva the tendon cells are separated by three lines of cells.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a comparison between embryo and larva.

claim: In the embryo, the P compartment is two cells wide.
source: Third, in the embryo, the P compartment is two cells wide, but it becomes about four cells wide in the larva (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: The P compartment becomes about four cells wide in the larva.
source: Third, in the embryo, the P compartment is two cells wide, but it becomes about four cells wide in the larva (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: These changes occur prior to the L2 stage and clearly involve a reorganisation of the cells that gives a substantial increase in length, along the anteroposterior axis.
source: These changes occur prior to the L2 stage and clearly involve a reorganisation of the cells that gives a substantial increase in length, along the anteroposterior axis (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 2.

claim: In spite of cell rearrangement, the cuticular pattern is very similar in all the three larval stages.
source: Nevertheless, in spite of this cell rearrangement, the cuticular pattern is very similar in all the three larval stages (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: Some cells must be reallocated to different fates during the transition from the embryo to the L2 larva.
source: suggesting that some cells must be reallocated to different fates during the transition from the embryo to the L2 larva.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the observation that pattern is conserved despite cell rearrangement.

claim: The number of cells in a defined rectangular portion of the segment remained constant in all three stages at a mean of about 73 cells.
source: The number of cells in a defined rectangular portion of the segment remained constant in all three stages at a mean of about 73 cells (Figure 2C–F), confirming that the epidermal cells do not divide or die.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 2, based on quantitative data.

claim: The epidermal cells do not divide or die.
source: The number of cells in a defined rectangular portion of the segment remained constant in all three stages at a mean of about 73 cells (Figure 2C–F), confirming that the epidermal cells do not divide or die.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the data showing constant cell number.

claim: In the embryo, the average number of lines of cells found in the anteroposterior axis of this portion was about 14.
source: In the embryo, the average number of lines of cells found in the anteroposterior axis of this portion was about 14 but it increased to 18 in the pre-L2 larva and remained unchanged thereafter and up to the pre-L3 stage (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 2, based on quantitative data.

claim: The number of lines of cells in the anteroposterior axis increased to 18 in the pre-L2 larva and remained unchanged thereafter and up to the pre-L3 stage.
source: In the embryo, the average number of lines of cells found in the anteroposterior axis of this portion was about 14 but it increased to 18 in the pre-L2 larva and remained unchanged thereafter and up to the pre-L3 stage (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 2, based on quantitative data.

claim: There was a large change in the shape of a fixed rectangle from the embryo to the L2 and L3 larval stages.
source: The ratios of the lengths of the anteroposterior to mediolateral axes were compared; there was a large change in the shape of this rectangle from the embryo to the L2 and L3 larval stages (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 2, based on quantitative measurements.

claim: Between the L1 and L2 larval stages, the ventral epithelial cells converge into the midline and extend in the anteroposterior axis.
source: Thus, both ways of describing the rearrangement of the cells argue that, between the L1 and L2 larval stages, the ventral epithelial cells converge into the midline and extend in the anteroposterior axis.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the quantitative data.

claim: This mode of cell rearrangement is known as convergent extension.
source: This mode of cell rearrangement is found in many systems and is known as convergent extension (reviewed in Keller, 2002; Wallingford et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to reviews.

claim: Clones induced soon after cellularisation usually divided one to two times during late embryogenesis, giving rise to small clones of marked cells.
source: To investigate in more detail how the cells rearrange, we induced clones soon after the time of cellularisation in the embryo and found these usually divided one to two times during late embryogenesis, giving rise to small clones of marked cells (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Table 1, based on experimental data.

claim: The number of cells per clone varied between one and four, or rarely five.
source: The number of cells per clone varied between one and four, or rarely five, (Table 1 and other clones studied but not included therein)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Table 1, based on experimental data.

claim: For each clone, the number of cells did not change significantly between the embryo (n = 404 cells) and the pre-L3 larva (n = 410).
source: and, for each clone (n = 121), this number did not change significantly between the embryo (n = 404 cells) and the pre-L3 larva (n = 410); confirming that cell divisions and cell death, if any, are rare in the larval epidermis.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on quantitative data from clone tracking.

claim: Cell divisions and cell death, if any, are rare in the larval epidermis.
source: and, for each clone (n = 121), this number did not change significantly between the embryo (n = 404 cells) and the pre-L3 larva (n = 410); confirming that cell divisions and cell death, if any, are rare in the larval epidermis.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the data showing constant cell numbers in clones.

claim: The lack of any epidermal cell death was confirmed by means of a caspase marker.
source: The lack of any epidermal cell death was confirmed by means of a caspase marker. The Apoliner marker stains apoptotic cells in embryos of stage 15 as previously reported (Bardet et al., 2008) and we found no cell death in the epidermis of L1 or L3 larvae (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by experimental data using a caspase marker and a citation.

claim: Single clones never extended across the ventral midline that divides left from right.
source: Single clones never extended across the ventral midline that divides left from right, presumably because any clone begins with a single cell that can only be on one side of the presumptive mesoderm.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations of clones.

claim: In the embryonic denticle belts, the constituent cells of every one of those clones were arranged in a line, parallel to the mediolateral axis.
source: Remarkably, in the embryonic denticle belts, the constituent cells of every one of those clones were arranged in a line, parallel to the mediolateral axis.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations of clone arrangements.

claim: Clones that were located in the naked cuticular region between the denticle belts tended to be much less aligned.
source: Note also that the cells in the denticulate area are strongly elongated in the mediolateral axis and closely packed. However, clones that were located in the naked cuticular region between the denticle belts tended to be much less aligned.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations of clone arrangements.

claim: The cells in the naked area, while still somewhat elongated in the mediolateral axis, were more isodiametric than those in the denticulate regions.
source: Also, the cells in the naked area, while still somewhat elongated in the mediolateral axis, were more isodiametric than those in the denticulate regions (Figures 2E and 4C).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to figures.

claim: The denticulate cells become aligned after they have been formed.
source: Perhaps the denticulate cells become aligned after they have been formed and, if so, it is intriguing that this movement is localised to only part of the segment.
evidence: The claim is stated as a speculation based on observations.

claim: Clone tracking demonstrated that the epithelial cells shift during postembryonic development and change their neighbours.
source: Clone tracking demonstrated that the epithelial cells shift during postembryonic development and change their neighbours.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a finding from clone tracking experiments.

claim: In every case any shift in the cells was anteriorwards.
source: In every case any shift in the cells was anteriorwards
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations from clone tracking.

claim: Line IV cells in the embryo are the source of the extra line of cells (IV') that is found between the two rows of muscle attachments in the larva.
source: for example the cells from line IV in the embryo contributed about equally to denticle rows 3 and 4 in the L3 larva (Figures 3D and 5)—observations arguing that line IV cells in the embryo are the source of the extra line of cells (IV') that is found between the two rows of muscle attachments in the larva.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an inference from clone tracking data and supported by figures.

claim: Line III, VI and VII do not rearrange but they do move forwards relative to the pattern.
source: Line III, VI and VII do not rearrange but they do move forwards relative to the pattern (see 'Cells change both identity and polarity').
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations from clone tracking.

claim: Cell lines II and V are the tendon cells, sites of muscle attachments in the embryo; in the larva they continue to be muscle attachments.
source: The other lines of cells are stable: cell lines II and V are the tendon cells, sites of muscle attachments in the embryo; in the larva they continue to be muscle attachments (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by reference to Figure 3.

claim: Of the cells producing denticles, many change their positions relative to the pattern as they develop from embryo to larva.
source: Taken together, as summarised in Figure 5, the clones show that, of the cells producing denticles, many change their positions relative to the pattern as they develop from embryo to larva.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary of clone tracking data and supported by Figure 5.

claim: All cell lines do not contribute equally to convergent extension, some cell lines turn into two cell lines in the larva, others make only one.
source: Also it is clear that all cell lines do not contribute equally to convergent extension, some cell lines turn into two cell lines in the larva, others make only one.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from clone tracking data.

claim: Clones within the naked cuticle are usually roundish or elongated in the anteroposterior axis (not in the mediolateral axis as are the denticulate clones).
source: Clones within the naked cuticle behave differently; first, they are usually roundish or elongated in the anteroposterior axis (not in the mediolateral axis as are the denticulate clones)
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations of clone shapes.

claim: Clones in the naked cuticle do not change much in overall shape between the embryo and L3.
source: second, the clones do not change much in overall shape between the embryo and L3.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations of clone shapes.

claim: There is also cell rearrangement in the naked cuticle.
source: The measurements mentioned above argue that there is also cell rearrangement in the naked cuticle.
evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from quantitative measurements.

claim: Nearly 30% of line I cells, which all form row 1 denticles in the late embryo and L1, moved forward to contribute to line I' and most of these produced row 0 denticles in L2 and L3.
source: Nearly 30% of line I cells, which all form row 1 denticles in the late embryo and L1, moved forward to contribute to line I' and most of these produced row 0 denticles in L2 and L3 (Figures 3A and 5; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures and Table 1, based on quantitative data.

claim: None of the 29 line –I cells checked made denticles of row 0 (or row 1) in L2 and L3.
source: We therefore checked the fate of 29 line –I cells and asked if any went on to make denticles of row 0 (or row 1) in L2 and L3. None of these cells made denticles in the larva and none joined line I' in the larva (Figures 5 and 4A; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures and Table 1, based on experimental data.

claim: All the row 0 denticles in line I' of the larva originate from cells that made row 1 denticles.
source: It appears therefore that all the row 0 denticles in line I' of the larva originate from cells that made row 1 denticles
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data on cell fates.

claim: Of 12 cells originating in line I (that made row 1 denticles in the embryo and became line I' in the larva), 2 failed to make denticles in the larva.
source: Even so, of 12 cells originating in line I (that made row 1 denticles in the embryo and became line I' in the larva), 2 failed to make denticles in the larva.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on quantitative data from cell tracking.

claim: Some individual line IV cells made row 4 denticles in the L1 stage but row 3 denticles in L2 and L3.
source: The most striking evidence for change of identity came from line IV cells. Some individual line IV cells made row 4 denticles in the L1 stage but row 3 denticles in L2 and L3 (Figures 3D and 5).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures, based on experimental data.

claim: Row 4 denticles point forwards and row 3 denticles point backwards.
source: Row 4 denticles point forwards and row 3 denticles point backwards.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a description of denticle polarity.

claim: An identified epidermal cell can undergo a change in overt polarity during normal larval development.
source: These cases prove that an identified epidermal cell, even as it grows in size and increases its DNA content without division, can undergo a change in overt polarity during normal larval development.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the observations on line IV cells.

claim: A change of polarity as a normal part of development has neither been suspected nor found before.
source: In an experimental situation involving ectopic expression of Dachsous, it was possible to change the polarity of epidermal cells as they developed through the larval stages (Repiso et al., 2010), but a change of polarity as a normal part of development has neither been suspected nor found before.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and contrasts normal development with experimental manipulation, supported by a citation.

claim: Line III cells made only row 3 denticles in L1 but all made row 2 denticles in L3.
source: Regarding the other lines of cells: cells from lines III, VI and VII were found to produce distinct types of denticles at different stages of development: line III cells made only row 3 denticles in L1 but all made row 2 denticles in L3 (Figures 3C and 5).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures, based on experimental data.

claim: Cells from lines VI and VII that made rows 6 and 7 denticles in the embryo made rows 5 and 6 denticles in the larva.
source: Similarly cells from lines VI and VII that made rows 6 and 7 denticles in the embryo made rows 5 and 6 denticles in the larva (Figures 3C, 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures, based on experimental data.

claim: Cells from lines II and V make row 2 and 5 denticles in the embryo but they do not make denticles at all in the larval stages.
source: Cells from lines II and V make row 2 and 5 denticles in the embryo but they do not make denticles at all in the larval stages (Figures 3B,D and 5).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures, based on experimental data.

claim: Single cells change their identity during normal development.
source: In so far as denticle position, size and polarity are tokens of cell identity, then these observations prove that single cells change their identity during normal development.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the observations on cell fate changes.

claim: There exist supracellular systems that act continuously to maintain a stable cuticular pattern in spite of considerable rearrangement of the cells.
source: Furthermore, the results argue for the existence of supracellular systems that act continuously to maintain a stable cuticular pattern in spite of considerable rearrangement of the cells (DiNardo et al., 1994; Heemskerk and Dinardo, 1994; Alexandre et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as an inference from the results and supported by citations.

claim: Although the embryonic tendon cells produce denticles, the larval tendon cells do not.
source: In order to maintain the same denticle pattern, the cells must compensate for changes in the behaviour of the tendon cells: we have shown that, although the embryonic tendon cells produce denticles (Hatini and DiNardo, 2001), the larval tendon cells do not.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of the stripe (sr) gene has two isoforms expressed at different times.
source: It may be relevant however that the expression of the stripe (sr) gene, that drives the differentiation of tendon cells, has two isoforms expressed at different times (Volohonsky et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: The embryonic tendon cells express the B isoform of sr.
source: The embryonic tendon cells express the B isoform of sr.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a description of gene expression.

claim: In the pre-L1 stage, when the muscles have already attached to the tendon cells and the pre-denticles have been formed, the tendon cells begin to express also the srA isoform.
source: Later, in the pre-L1 stage, when the muscles have already attached to the tendon cells and the pre-denticles have been formed, the tendon cells begin to express also the srA isoform (Frommer et al., 1996; Becker et al., 1997; Vorbruggen and Jackle, 1997).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations.

claim: The early expression of either srA or srB failed to block the formation of pre-denticles and denticles in L1.
source: To test we expressed srA and srB prematurely and ectopically in the early embryo in clones and found that the early expression of either of these forms failed to block the formation of pre-denticles and denticles in L1.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on experimental data.

claim: In the larva, cells in clones over-expressing either SrA or SrB acquired the actin palisades characteristic of muscle-attached tendon cells in L3 and did not form any denticles.
source: However, in the larva, cells in those clones over-expressing either SrA or SrB acquired the actin palisades characteristic of muscle-attached tendon cells in L3 (Figure 1B,D) and did not form any denticles (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by figures, based on experimental data.

claim: Although sr expression allows denticle formation in the embryo, it blocks denticle formation in the larva.
source: One simple interpretation is that, although sr expression allows denticle formation in the embryo, it blocks denticle formation in the larva.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: There is no case of cells producing row 2 (A compartment) in the embryo that make row 1 denticles (P compartment) in the larva.
source: Indeed there is no case of cells producing row 2 (A compartment) in the embryo that make row 1 denticles (P compartment) in the larva, even though this would only require a small anteriorwards shift in cell fate, as happens to other lines of cells.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated based on observations from cell tracking.

claim: Wild type cells that are adjacent to a nascent clone of cells lacking the frizzled gene form hairs of reversed polarity.
source: For example, wild type cells that are adjacent to a nascent clone of cells lacking the frizzled gene form hairs of reversed polarity (Gubb and Garcia-Bellido, 1982).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation.

claim: During development from embryo to larva, cells, as a consequence of rearrangement, acquire new neighbours.
source: During development from embryo to larva, we have shown that cells, as a consequence of rearrangement, acquire new neighbours.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a finding from the study.

claim: If new neighbours were to present different amounts of Dachsous or Fat on their abutting membranes, this would lead to different arrangements of heterodimers and consequent polarity changes.
source: Moreover, if these new neighbours were to present different amounts of Dachsous or Fat on their abutting membranes, this would lead to different arrangements of heterodimers and consequent polarity changes (Ma et al., 2003; Casal et al., 2006; Repiso et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is stated as a mechanistic explanation and supported by citations.

claim: Two lines of cells that make denticles in L1 do not make denticles in L2/3.
source: Comparison is problematic because we have shown that two lines of cells that make denticles in L1 do not make denticles in L2/3.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a finding from the study.

claim: The two replacement denticular rows in L2/3 must be made by cells that either did not have denticular identity in L1, or by cells that contributed to different denticle rows in L1.
source: Since the number of denticle rows is about the same in all three larval stages, it follows that the two replacement denticular rows in L2/3 must be made by cells that either did not have denticular identity in L1, or by cells that contributed to different denticle rows in L1.
evidence: The claim is stated as a logical inference from the observation that the number of rows is constant.

claim: The functional outcome of the developmental processes described is the segmented pattern of denticle bands.
source: The functional outcome of the developmental processes we describe is the segmented pattern of denticle bands.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as a summary of the functional significance.

claim: The denticle band pattern appears to be important for crawling.
